There are no slides for this lecture. The page is built from the lecture notes (green — study guide written from Dr. Sultan's lecture by Mohammed Alessa, Mohammed Alsalamah & Abdulrahman Alomar) and every gift (red). Aldughaither has no aneurysm chapter.

Three ideas that organize everything

  • 1 · Location → complication: aortic and visceral aneurysms rupture; limb (peripheral) aneurysms thrombose and embolize.
  • 2 · Laplace drives growth: wall tension = pressure × radius → ↑ radius or BP → ↑ tension → more dilatation → rupture. Size and growth rate set the risk.
  • 3 · When to repair: when the expected rupture risk exceeds the operative risk (elective open AAA repair ≈ 5% mortality).

1. Definition & classification

  • Aneurysm = localized arterial dilatation ≥ 50% greater than the adjacent normal diameter. Arteriomegaly = diffuse enlargement (not focal). AAA = abdominal aortic diameter ≥ 3 cm (~1% of people > 50; ~8% in high-risk groups). Overall prevalence ~1–8%; less common in women.
True aneurysmFalse aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm)
WallAll 3 layers — intima, media, adventitiaWall breach; the sac lacks the 3 layers
MechanismDilatation of a weakened but intact wallBlood escapes through a defect into a contained sac
CauseDegenerative (most), genetic, inflammatory, infectiveTrauma or arterial puncture (e.g. femoral catheterization)
ShapeFusiform (circumferential) or saccular (one-sided)Sac connected to the artery by a neck

Aetiology

CauseNotes
Degenerative (most common)Weakened elastic lamina/media, ↑ protease activity → collagen/elastin breakdown
Genetic / connective tissueMarfan, Ehlers-Danlos
Inflammatory (non-infective)Lymphocyte/plasma-cell infiltration; thick whitish wall; e.g. arthritis, chronic pancreatitis
Infectious (mycotic)Salmonella (classic), Brucella (Saudi Arabia — unpasteurized dairy); fever common
OtherCongenital, post-stenotic, post-dissection, trauma, iatrogenic
  • Mycotic: blood cultures may be negative → send tissue cultures. Treatment: excise/debride + antibiotics + reconstruction (in-situ graft or extra-anatomic bypass, e.g. axillo-femoral, away from the infected field).

Distribution & natural history

  • Most → least common: 1 infrarenal abdominal aorta → 2 popliteal → 3 thoracic aorta → 4 femoral → 5 carotid and others. Iliac involvement often accompanies AAA.
  • Growth ~1–2 mm/year or irregular spurts → surveillance. Turbulent flow → mural thrombus → distal embolization (especially peripheral aneurysms). Enlargement compresses veins, nerves and organs.
  • Most common site of abdominal aortic aneurysm → infrarenal aorta (answer recalled without the question). 435

2. Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA)

Risk of developing AAAFactors that raise rupture concern
Advanced age, male sexLarger diameter, rapid expansion
Smoking (dose-dependent, pack-years)Continued smoking, COPD
HypertensionRising wall tension (Laplace)
Atherosclerotic/cardiovascular diseaseFemale sex — rupture at smaller diameters
  • Partner aneurysm (EXAM): ~50% of patients with a femoral/popliteal aneurysm have an AAA → in every AAA check femoral and popliteal pulses; with any peripheral aneurysm look for an AAA.

Presentation

  • Most are asymptomatic — found incidentally on US/CT. Symptomatic unruptured: persistent deep abdominal or back pain; large ones compress the duodenum, kidneys, ureters.
  • Ruptured AAA — classic triad: severe abdominal/back pain + hypotension/shock + pulsatile abdominal mass. Examination is insensitive (< 50% diagnosed clinically).
  • The most common presentation of AAA → incidental finding. 437 ×4
  • A pulsating abdominal mass (in the acute setting) indicates → rupture of an AAA. 442
Added explanationAorto-enteric fistula — usually secondary (after aortic graft surgery, typically to the 3rd/4th duodenum) presenting with a "herald" GI bleed; primary fistulas (an untreated AAA eroding into bowel) also exist — so it is not "always" after surgery.
  • Aorto-enteric fistula — the false statement → "always after surgery for AAA". 426

Investigations

ModalityRoleNote
UltrasoundScreening of choice; bedside check in suspected ruptureCheap, no radiation; limited by obesity and bowel gas
CT / CTADiagnosis, anatomy and operative planningMeasure perpendicular to the centreline (oblique cuts overestimate)
Conventional angiographyMainly during interventionUnderestimates size — shows only the lumen, not the mural thrombus
  • Investigation used to diagnose an aortic aneurysm → keyed duplex ultrasound (the screening/diagnostic test; CT then plans repair). 438

Indications for repair

  • Diameter ≥ 5.5 cm in men, ≥ 5.0 cm in women.
  • Rapid expansion (EXAM): ≥ 0.5 cm in 6 months or ≥ 1 cm per year.
  • Symptomatic (persistent pain, other causes excluded) → urgent repair after optimization. Ruptured → immediate emergency repair.
  • Small and asymptomatic → surveillance + cardiovascular risk control; medical treatment doesn't reverse dilatation.
  • Size indicating surgery → 5.5 cm. 441
  • Incidental aneurysm managed conservatively → 4 cm. 439
  • Incidental AAA — indication for surgery → symptomatic (not 3.5–4 cm or hypertension). 437

EVAR vs open repair

  • Goal: exclude the sac from arterial pressure and flow.
EVAROpen repair
HowStent-graft inside the aorta; main body + contralateral limb under fluoroscopyReplace the segment with a sewn-in tube or bifurcated graft
NeedsSuitable proximal and distal landing zones, neck and access vesselsNot dependent on landing zones
AdvantagesSmaller incisions, less blood loss, lower morbidity, shorter stayNo long-term imaging surveillance
DrawbacksLifelong surveillance (annual CT), graft-related problemsHigher early morbidity; elective mortality ≈ 5%
Specific complicationsEndoleak, limb occlusion, graft thrombosis, access-site problemsRenal failure, MI, limb ischaemia, colonic ischaemia, erectile dysfunction
  • Open repair in 5 steps: clamp above and below → open the sac → control lumbar bleeders → insert the graft → close the sac over the graft.

Ruptured AAA — emergency management

  • Recognize (pain + shock ± tender pulsatile mass) → resuscitate and mobilize (ABC, 2 large-bore lines, crossmatch, massive transfusion protocol, call vascular/OR/anaesthesia/ICU) → image (unstable → bedside US; stable → CTA only if it won't delay) → emergency open or endovascular repair.
  • Permissive hypotension: don't normalize BP before control — SBP ≈ 90 mmHg is acceptable if perfusion is maintained. ~50% mortality even among those reaching hospital.
  • Pulsatile epigastric mass with BP 80/60 → keyed immediate laparotomy (straight to theatre — don't delay for CT). 430

3. Thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA)

AAATAA
FrequencyMost common (infrarenal)Less common
CausesDegenerativeDegenerative; post-dissection, connective tissue disease, inflammatory, infection
Risk factorsAge, male, smoking, HTN, CVDSmoking, alcohol, age, HTN, COPD; familial
ImagingUS screens; CTA plansCTA (US limited)
Repair≥ 5.5 cm men / ≥ 5.0 cm women; symptomatic; rupture; rapid growth~6 cm; symptomatic; rupture; rapid expansion (~1 cm/yr)
EndovascularEVARTEVAR (open/hybrid if anatomy requires)
Signature riskEndoleak; bowel/renal ischaemia, EDSpinal cord ischaemia / paraplegia, stroke
  • TAA presentation: mostly asymptomatic; chest/back/flank pain; compression — oesophagus → dysphagia; trachea → respiratory symptoms; nerves → voice changes (recurrent laryngeal → hoarseness).
  • Spinal cord ischaemia: spinal perfusion pressure ≈ MAP − CSF pressure → keep MAP up and drain CSF; monitor leg movement post-op.
  • Symptom distinguishing a thoracic from an abdominal aneurysm → cough and hoarseness (compression of the airway/recurrent laryngeal nerve). 441

4. Peripheral arterial aneurysms

  • ~70% of peripheral aneurysms are popliteal. Most are asymptomatic; thrombosis and distal embolization are the major complications (rupture uncommon); compression of veins (→ DVT) and nerves.
  • Ischaemic cascade: turbulent flow → mural thrombus → thrombosis/embolization → acute limb ischaemia. Thrombus is chronic/organized → thrombolysis/thrombectomy work poorly → poor limb salvage.

Popliteal aneurysm

  • Repair when symptomatic (embolization, thrombosis, compression) or ~2–2.5 cm; acute thrombosis → emergency intervention.
  • Preferred: surgical exclusion + autologous (reversed) vein bypass; alternatives prosthetic graft or stent-graft (stents kink/fracture with knee flexion).

Femoral aneurysm & pseudoaneurysm

  • True femoral aneurysms are uncommon; pseudoaneurysms are often iatrogenic after femoral catheterization (deep, hard to compress, obesity) — US-guided puncture reduces them. Mycotic pseudoaneurysms in IV drug users. Complications: thrombosis/embolization, femoral nerve and vein compression.
  • Imaging: duplex first (size, flow, neck, thrombus, true vs false) → CTA/MRA if needed; arteriography during intervention.
Pseudoaneurysm treatmentHowNote
US-guided compressionPressure over the neck → sac thrombosisNon-invasive
US-guided thrombin injectionThrombin into the sacNarrow neck only — a wide neck lets thrombin into the parent artery
Surgical repairDirect open repairWhen percutaneous methods fail/unsuitable

Upper-limb aneurysms

  • Subclavian: degenerative, post-stenotic dilatation, clavicular trauma, arterial thoracic outlet syndrome (compression between the 1st/cervical rib and scalenes) → aneurysm → recurrent distal emboli → digital ischaemia. Main concern = embolization, not rupture. Treatment: resection + reconstruction or stent-graft.
  • Radial: usually pseudoaneurysms after catheterization (less common than femoral — superficial, compressible against bone). Allen's test before ligation: adequate ulnar collateral → ligation; inadequate → reconstruction.

5. Visceral artery aneurysms

  • Splenic (~60%) → hepatic → SMA, renal. Rupture is the main danger. Multiple visceral aneurysms → suspect infection or vasculitis.
SplenicHepaticSMARenal
WhoMost common; women; FMD, portal hypertension2nd; menUncommon; often mycoticWomen; saccular at the 1st bifurcation; FMD
HallmarkPregnancy rupture (3rd trimester): ~75% maternal, ~90% fetal mortalityHaemobilia triad: abdominal pain + GI bleeding + jaundice; rupture mortality ~35%Rupture, bowel ischaemia, fistulaRenovascular hypertension (RAAS)
Repair> 2 cm, symptomatic, or woman of childbearing ageBy site/anatomyBy location and branch importance> 2 cm, childbearing age, uncontrolled HTN, symptomatic
TreatmentCoils/covered stent; hilar → may need splenectomyLigation OK if collaterals (portal flow 70–75%)No endografts in infection; preserve major branchesStent-graft or reconstruction

Size thresholds at a glance

  • AAA defined ≥ 3 cm (diagnosis) · repair AAA ≥ 5.0 cm (women) / ≥ 5.5 cm (men) · TAA ~6 cm · popliteal ~2–2.5 cm or symptomatic · splenic & renal > 2 cm (or childbearing age).

Mastery checklist (notes)

  • Aortic and visceral aneurysms rupture; limb aneurysms thrombose and embolize.
  • Most common site: infrarenal aorta → popliteal → thoracic → femoral.
  • ~50% with a femoral/popliteal aneurysm have an AAA.
  • US screens; CTA plans (measure perpendicular); angiography underestimates.
  • Repair AAA ≥ 5.5 cm men / ≥ 5.0 cm women, growth ≥ 0.5 cm/6 mo or ≥ 1 cm/yr, symptomatic, ruptured.
  • EVAR needs landing zones and lifelong surveillance (endoleak); open repair risks colonic ischaemia and ED.
  • Ruptured AAA: massive transfusion, permissive hypotension (SBP ~90), straight to repair.
  • TAA repair ~6 cm; TEVAR; spinal cord ischaemia — keep MAP up, drain CSF.
  • Popliteal: repair ~2–2.5 cm or symptomatic; vein bypass preferred.
  • Pseudoaneurysm: compression, thrombin (narrow neck only), or surgery.
  • Splenic: women, pregnancy rupture; hepatic: haemobilia triad.
